description: A lightweight winter jacket filled with recycled down and wrapped in a windproof shell. Tested in the Norwegian mountains down to minus twenty degrees. Packs into its own pocket, so it lives in a rucksack without taking the space of a second coat.

A double-breasted peacoat cut from heavy Merino wool spun in Portugal. The collar stands up against coastal wind and the lining is quilted for winter commuting. Traditional tailoring, and heavy enough to feel like it will outlast the wearer.

A packable rain shell with taped seams and pit zips for hard walking. It sheds a downpour without turning into a sauna, which is the usual complaint about cheaper waterproofs. Hood adjusts with one hand while the other holds a map.

A mid-layer fleece made from recycled bottles, brushed on the inside for warmth without bulk. Wears well under a shell in winter and on its own through a mild spring. The zip pockets are deep enough to actually keep a phone.

An enamelled cast iron pot that goes from hob to oven to table. Holds heat long after the flame is off, which is what makes a slow braise work. Heavy, and deliberately so: the lid seals under its own weight and keeps moisture in.

A carbon steel chef knife forged in Solingen and finished by hand. Takes a sharper edge than stainless and holds it longer, at the cost of needing to be dried after every wash. For anyone who cooks daily it is the only knife on the board.

Three copper saucepans lined with stainless steel, so they respond to heat instantly without reacting with the food. Sauces that split in thin aluminium behave here. They need polishing, and they look worth polishing.
A glazed stoneware dish that bakes evenly and comes to the table without apology. Deep enough for a lasagne for six. Survived a year of daily use in our test kitchen with no crazing in the glaze.

An articulated desk lamp in brushed brass with a warm dimmable LED. The arm holds its position rather than drifting down over an evening, which is the failing of most cheap copies. Casts light on the page and not in the eyes.

A hand-blown opal glass globe that diffuses light softly in every direction. Hangs over a dining table without glare. Each one varies slightly, which is what happens when glass is blown rather than moulded.
A tall floor lamp that leans over an armchair to put light exactly where a book is. Weighted base so it does not tip when the shade is pushed forward. Warm enough at night not to wake anyone up.

A task chair with a mesh back that flexes with the spine instead of fighting it. Every axis adjusts, including the ones most chairs leave fixed. Expensive, and cheaper than a back specialist after two years at a desk.

A solid oak desk with a single shallow drawer and no cable tray, on the argument that cables should be dealt with rather than hidden. The grain is finished with hardwax oil so a scratch can be rubbed out rather than repaired.
Open larch shelving that can be wall-fixed or left freestanding. Holds books at every shelf height without bowing, which is the test a lot of flat-pack shelving fails in its second year.

A low armchair upholstered in heavy Belgian linen over a beech frame. The cushions are feather-wrapped foam, so they keep their shape but still give. Loose covers come off for washing, which matters with pets.

A full-grain leather boot with a resoleable welt, built for multi-day walking under a loaded pack. Stiff for the first week, then moulds to the foot and stays that way for years. Waterproof without a membrane to fail.
A hand-stitched deck shoe in salt-resistant nubuck with a siped rubber sole that grips a wet deck. Wears in rather than out. The laces are rawhide and will outlive the fashion for them.
A knitted everyday trainer with a cork footbed that takes the shape of the wearer. Light enough to walk a city all day. The upper is a single piece, so there are no seams to rub.
A hand grinder with ceramic burrs that produce an even grind without heating the beans. Adjusts from espresso to French press by feel. Quiet enough to use before anyone else in the house is awake.
A borosilicate glass teapot with a removable steel infuser, so the leaves come out when the tea is ready rather than stewing. Watching the colour develop is half the point of brewing loose leaf.
An end-grain oak board that closes around the knife edge instead of blunting it. A channel round the rim catches juices from a roast. Needs oiling monthly and will then last decades.

A waxed canvas backpack with bridle leather straps and a roll top that keeps rain out of a laptop. Ages into something better looking than it started. The base is double-layered where bags usually wear through first.
A dense wool felt sleeve that protects a laptop inside a larger bag. No zip to scratch the lid. Slim enough that it does not turn a backpack into a suitcase.
A two-night duffel in waxed canvas with a leather base that can be set down on wet ground. Fits under an aircraft seat. The shoulder strap is wide enough to carry loaded without cutting in.

A knee-length parka using the same recycled down as the Alpine Down Jacket, in a heavier shell for standing about rather than moving. Cut long enough to wear over the Harbour Wool Peacoat on the worst days. Nordhaus Textiles fill every jacket in the same Oslo workshop.

Waterproof overtrousers built as the companion to the Trailhead Rain Shell, in the same ripstop nylon and the same taped seams. Full-length side zips go on over the Trailmark Hiking Boot without taking the boot off, which is the whole point of them.

A sleeveless version of the Riverbank Fleece for people who run warm through the arms. Layers under the Trailhead Rain Shell with no bunching at the shoulder. Same recycled polyester, same deep zip pockets.

The small companion to the Ferro Chef Knife 20cm, forged from the same carbon steel in the same Solingen workshop. Handles the work a chef knife is too big for. Like its larger sibling it must be dried after washing.

A cast iron skillet from the same foundry as the Kettle Cast Dutch Oven, pre-seasoned and ready to use. Goes from hob to oven for a frittata. Pairs with the Ridge Chopping Board, which is wide enough to rest it on.

A tall copper stockpot lined in stainless steel, matching the Copperline Saucepan Set it is designed to stand beside. Big enough for stock from a whole chicken. Wants the same polishing as the rest of the range.

A shallower glazed dish from the same Tessera Ceramics range as the Stoneware Baking Dish, in a diameter meant for a pie rather than a lasagne. The same glaze, which has come through a year of daily use uncrazed.

The Meridian Desk Lamp arm on a clamp instead of a base, for a desk with no surface to spare. Fits the edge of the Oak Writing Desk without marking the oil finish. Same warm dimmable LED and the same joint that holds its position.
Three hand-blown globes on a shared brass bar, the Pendant Globe Light multiplied for a longer table. Each globe varies slightly, so a row of three is visibly hand-made rather than stamped out.
A slim steel picture light from the makers of the Reading Floor Lamp, on the same warm dimming circuit. Throws an even wash across a canvas without a hotspot in the middle.

A high stool using the Cirrus Ergonomic Chair mesh and gas lift, for a standing desk or a workbench. The footring is where a chair would have castors. Shares every adjustment the chair has except the recline.
A small solid oak table finished in the same hardwax oil as the Oak Writing Desk, so the two age at the same rate. Sized to sit beside the Linen Armchair at the height of its arm.
A low larch cabinet built on the Larch Shelving Unit frame, with two sliding doors for the things that should not be on display. Holds its shelf line without bowing under a record collection.
The Linen Armchair widened to two seats, in the same heavy Belgian linen over the same beech frame. Loose covers come off for washing. Feather-wrapped foam cushions, so it gives without collapsing.
A steam-bent beech dining chair from the frame shop that makes the Linen Armchair. Stacks four high. Sits comfortably for the length of a long dinner, which is more than most dining chairs manage.
A low-cut approach shoe using the Trailmark Hiking Boot sole compound on a lighter suede upper. For the walk in, when the boot is more than the ground asks for. Takes the same Trailmark Gaiters.
An ankle boot in the salt-resistant nubuck of the Harbour Deck Shoe, with the same siped sole for a wet deck. Higher cut for spray. The rawhide laces are shared with the deck shoe.
The Citypath Trainer without the laces, on the same cork footbed that moulds to the wearer. Seamless knit upper, so nothing rubs. For the short walks where lacing a shoe is the obstacle.
A weighted tamper sized to the basket, the natural companion to the Slate Coffee Grinder once the grind is fine enough for espresso. Heavy enough that the weight does the work rather than the wrist.
A borosilicate carafe from the same range as the Glasshouse Teapot, for water on a dinner table or cold brew in a fridge. Pours without dribbling down the side, which is rarer than it should be.
A larger end-grain board than the Ridge Chopping Board, with a deeper juice channel for a roast. Kind to the Ferro Chef Knife 20cm in the same way. Oil it monthly and it outlives the kitchen.
Six stoneware plates in the glaze used on the Stoneware Baking Dish, so the dish can come straight to the table among them. Stack without chipping and take a dishwasher without dulling.
Four stoneware mugs matching the Tessera Dinner Plates, thick-walled so coffee from the Slate Coffee Grinder stays hot to the bottom. The handle takes a whole hand, not two fingers.

The Field Canvas Backpack in a holdall shape, same waxed canvas and same bridle leather. Carries by hand or on the shoulder. The doubled base is the part of the Weekender Duffel that people notice first.
A dense wool felt tote from the makers of the Commuter Laptop Sleeve, cut to hold the sleeve exactly. No zip, on the argument that a tote with a zip is a bag pretending to be something else.
Ripstop gaiters that seal the gap above the Trailmark Hiking Boot and fit the Trailmark Approach Shoe as well. Made from the same fabric as the Trailhead Rain Shell, so they pack down to nothing.
